passage: Week one: the product team of five sat under a new poster that said TRUST IS OUR SUPERPOWER. Nobody spoke first at stand-up. Akash promised to update the shared tracker by six, and he did, that same evening, though no one commented. Week two, Wednesday: before the review, Akash messaged the group, 'I entered the wrong launch date in the tracker yesterday. Fixed now, sorry for the confusion.' Leela, who usually stayed silent, replied that she had a similar slip in her test notes and had fixed hers too. Week four, Friday: at the demo, the manager praised the smooth rollout. Akash said, 'Leela caught the login bug on Tuesday. That one was hers.' Afterwards, two teammates who had kept to themselves asked Leela to look over their code before Monday.

qa.q: What did Akash promise to do in week one?
qa.a: He promised to update the shared tracker by six, and he did it that same evening.

qa.q: Why might Leela have admitted her own slip after Akash's message?
qa.a: She probably felt safer and less afraid of being judged, because Akash had just owned his mistake openly before anyone found it.

qa.q: What small habit could the manager encourage so the trust keeps growing?
qa.a: Keep small promises visible, like a quick note when a task is done or an error is fixed, instead of adding more posters.

qa.q: How might the two quieter teammates see the team by week four?
qa.a: They seem to see a place where mistakes are named and credit is shared fairly, so they now feel safe asking Leela for help.

passage: Nandini, you're worried your new team doesn't trust you. Let your Jatin chacha tell you about the dye works in Surat. When the big export order went out clean, the owner thanked me, and I told him the night shift deserved it. Small things, beta. Nobody remembers that banner.

qa.q: What did the owner hang up that changed nothing?
qa.a: A banner about unity.

qa.a: Jatin admitting the maroon batch mistake first; it showed that owning an error was safe, so Hameed and the others began to do the same.

qa.q: What might the night shift have felt when Jatin gave them credit for the clean order?
qa.a: After being blamed every morning, they likely felt surprised and respected, finally seen for their work.

grounding: An uncle's memory showing that trust on a work team came from admitting errors early and sharing credit, not from a banner.

Afreen sighed. 'The client emailed me late. I thought if I didn't fix it right away, we'd look bad.'
'That makes sense. So what if late changes go in our group chat, and whoever is free picks them up?'
Rakesh stopped typing. 'I'm usually up late anyway. I'll take the night ones.'

passage: Last term, three of us new teachers shared one projector, and Charu had it almost every day. Mona and Deepak grumbled about it at lunch, but never to Charu. I was tired of teaching my Class 8 map lesson on a chalkboard. So one Friday I said, 'Charu, can I talk about the projector? No one ever said.' That stung, because she was partly right. We sat with the timetable and made a sign-up sheet for the staffroom door. Mona wrote her name on it first. qa.a: Instead of grumbling at lunch, they could name the problem directly, say how it affects them and ask for the other person's view.

qa.a: Mona had only grumbled before, so she likely felt relieved to have a fair turn at last, which is why she wrote her name first.
